memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text:
"'Anyone who injures their neighbour is to be injured in the same
manner: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth. The one
who has inflicted the injury must suffer the same injury'"
- Lev 24:19-20 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
"Eye for eye" is often quoted as if it were a licence for revenge. It
was the opposite. In a world where a family might wipe out a village
over a single insult, this law set a ceiling: the punishment could not
exceed the injury. It was given to judges, not to angry individuals.

That is an important distinction. This was Israel's court system putting
limits on retaliation, ensuring that penalties were proportionate rather
than escalating.

Dear reader, Jesus addressed how people had twisted it. He said, you have
heard that it was said, eye for eye and tooth for tooth. But I tell you,
do not resist an evil person (Matt 5:38-39). He was not overturning
justice in the courts; He was confronting personal vengeance in the
heart.

That is much harder than it sounds. Something in us keeps a careful
ledger of wounds and waits for the chance to settle accounts.

Paul writes, do not repay anyone evil for evil... do not take revenge,
but leave room for God's wrath (Rom 12:17-19). Notice the reason he
gives: God will handle it. We can release our claim because justice is
not being abandoned, only handed to better hands.

And at the cross we see this perfectly. When Jesus was insulted, He did
not retaliate but entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly (1 Pet
2:23).

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. What wound am I still keeping an account of?
2. Am I willing to entrust justice to God rather than settling it
   myself?
3. Who do I need to release from my ledger this week?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Lord, I hand over the accounts I have been keeping. Give me grace not to
repay evil for evil, and help me trust You to judge justly. Amen.
